title: Microsoft Outlook and Workplace Email Habits
summary: By the end, learners can open Outlook Mail and Calendar, write and send a message, choose Reply, Reply All, or Forward with care, use To, Cc, Bcc, and attachments, follow Microsoft’s basic professional-email habits, and create a simple appointment or meeting.

lessons.title: What Outlook is and how to start a message
lessons.html:
Microsoft Outlook is a program that keeps email, calendars, contacts, and tasks in one place. Microsoft’s basic-tasks guide says that after you set up an account you can send and receive email, use the calendar, save contacts, and work with tasks.

The first time you start Outlook, it may ask for your name, email address, and password. That is often enough. If setup fails, Outlook may ask for more details, such as a mail server name, which your email provider can give you. You can add another account later from File > Add Account. Do not enter a real password into this course — practise only on an account your tutor or workplace has approved.

A quick access or navigation area lets you move among Mail, Calendar, People, and Tasks.

To write a new email (Microsoft):

  1. From a mail folder such as your Inbox, choose New Email. (A keyboard shortcut Microsoft lists is Ctrl+Shift+M.)
  2. Add recipients, a subject, and your message.
  3. Choose Send when you are done.

The Inbox is where new mail usually arrives. Click a message to read it in the reading pane or open it fully.

If Outlook is not on the computer in front of you, ask your adult learning council which version they have. This course is not MOS training and not a tech-support contract.

lessons.title: Reply, Reply All, or Forward
lessons.html:
When you receive a message, Microsoft lists three common actions:

  • Reply sends your new message only to the original sender. Attachments from the original message are not included.
  • Reply All sends your new message to the original sender and everyone on the original To and Cc lines. Attachments are not included.
  • Forward lets you send the message to new people. Attachments from the original message are included automatically.

You will find Reply, Reply All, and Forward on the ribbon, beside the message, or at the top of the reading pane, depending on your screen and Outlook version.

Microsoft asks you to think before you choose Reply All, especially if the message went to many people. It is often better to choose Reply and then add only the people who truly need your answer. If you do use Reply All, remove anyone who does not need the message.

After you choose an option:

  1. Write your message.
  2. Add or remove names in the To, Cc, or Bcc boxes if needed.
  3. Check the subject line. A reply usually starts with RE: and a forward with FW: — you can change the subject if you want.
  4. Select Send.

If you reply and later need to send a file, attach it yourself. If you need to pass the original files to someone new, Forward is the action that keeps those attachments.

lessons.title: To, Cc, Bcc, and attachments
lessons.html:
The address boxes tell Outlook who should get the message.

Microsoft’s “write great email” guidance says:

  • Put people who need to respond or take action on the To line.
  • Put people who need to be informed on the Cc line.
  • Limit the message to people who need to read it.

Bcc means blind carbon copy. When you put someone on the Bcc line, they receive a copy, but other recipients do not see that person’s name. In new Outlook, Microsoft’s steps include Options > Show fields > Show Bcc. In classic Outlook, you can choose Options > Bcc (or Bcc on the ribbon if you are writing in the reading pane).

Microsoft also warns: a Bcc recipient might reply to everyone by mistake and reveal they were copied. Do not use Bcc to secretly copy a manager on a sensitive note — Microsoft says it is safer to forward the sent message afterward if that person needs to know.

To attach a file (Microsoft):

  1. Create a message, or choose Reply, Reply All, or Forward.
  2. Choose Attach File (on the Message tab in some views).
  3. Pick the file, then Send.

To save an attachment you receive, select it and choose Save As (or right-click and Save As). Open unexpected attachments with care — see the Range Path email-safety course if a file looks suspicious.

Never attach something you would not want a wider group to see.

lessons.title: Write a clear, professional message
lessons.html:
Knowing the buttons is only half the skill. Microsoft publishes “do’s and don’ts” for professional email in Outlook.

Do:

  • Read your message before you send it.
  • Write a descriptive, action-oriented subject, such as who it is for and what you need. Useful openings Microsoft mentions include “FYI:” and “Action Required.”
  • If the topic of a long conversation changes, change the subject.
  • Keep messages short and to the point. Put the most important information first.
  • Put questions or action items on their own lines so they stand out.
  • Use a signature when it fits, but keep it simple, short, and professional.
  • If you cannot give a full answer yet, send a short note that you are looking into it and will reply by a certain time.

Don’t (from the same Microsoft list):

  • Write in ALL CAPS.
  • Send a message while you are angry — better to save a draft and come back later.
  • Mark every message as High Importance; people will start to ignore it.
  • Use sarcasm, which is easy to misunderstand.
  • Write something you would not want others at work to read.
  • Reply All to a large group only to ask to be removed from a list.

These are workplace habits, not law. Your employer may have extra rules. When in doubt, keep the note short, polite, and clear.

If a problem needs a fast answer, Microsoft notes that a phone call or instant message can work better than a long email.

lessons.title: Calendar, meetings, and your signature
lessons.html:
Outlook’s Calendar helps you track your time. Microsoft makes a clear difference:

  • An appointment is something you put on your own calendar that does not invite other people or book a room. In a Calendar folder, choose New Appointment (or right-click a time and choose New Appointment).
  • A meeting includes other people and can include a room or other resources. Choose New Meeting. Replies to the meeting request arrive in your Inbox.

You can set a reminder so a notice appears before the appointment or meeting. Open the item and choose how much time before it you want the reminder — or choose None to turn it off.

To create a signature (Microsoft):

  1. In a new message, choose Signature > Signatures.
  2. On the Email Signature tab, choose New, type a name, and choose OK.
  3. You can set a default signature for new messages and, if you want, for replies and forwards.
  4. Under Edit signature, type the text and choose OK.

Microsoft’s professional-email guidance says to keep a signature simple, short, professional, and, if possible, free of large graphics.

A simple workplace signature might be your name, job title, and phone number — only details your workplace is comfortable sharing.

When you finish class, sign out if you are on a shared computer. Ask staff before you change settings on a learning-centre account.
